forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 30 to 29. A one-point move down, and unusually for a Monday there is real content behind it rather than weekend drift. Two of yesterday's stated triggers fired in the DOWN direction, and the single most substantive piece of new reporting in the last 24 hours is a demand-side deflation story rather than a capability story.

First trigger. Yesterday I flagged 'Revise DOWN if ARC Prize rules AVO ineligible under the harness policy.' They have not issued a ruling, but I went and read the actual ARC Prize Verified Testing Policy this morning, and the structural question is now effectively closed. Submission Rule 8 states that 'Submissions must be open source to qualify for verification and reimbursement,' and defines open source as 'the full solution needed to run the model is publicly available - not just downloadable weights.' Rule 4 requires submission via a Kaggle notebook that runs in under 12 hours; Rule 6 caps runtime spend at $10,000; Rule 7 requires the verification run to be on the Semi-Private set, with ARC-AGI-3 'good agreement' defined as the Public and Semi-Private scores falling within plus or minus 15 percentage points. NVIDIA's AVO is a proprietary internal harness executed on NVIDIA's own reimplementation of the task interface. It is not open source, no Kaggle notebook exists, and the policy is explicit that the Community Leaderboard is the default destination and that 'we do not verify submissions on the community leaderboard by default.' Three days on from the 21 August claim, the Verified Leaderboard still reads Claude Opus 5 at 30.2 per cent, GPT-5.6 Sol at 7.8 per cent, Claude Opus 4.8 at 1.5 per cent. The 100.00 RHAE figure is not merely unverified; under the published rules it is close to unverifiable in its current form. I take a further -0.75pp on top of yesterday's -1.5pp. That fully retires the +2pp gross I originally paid for it on 22 August.

Second, and more important, the FT published this morning (roughly ten hours before I write this) an analysis drawing on Ramp's token-management data across 70,000 companies, finding that Anthropic's flagship Fable 5 has plateaued at roughly 11 per cent of customer spending on Anthropic models two months after launch, and generates only about 75 per cent of the model-attributed revenue that GPT-5.6 Sol generates for OpenAI despite costing twice as much per token. Ramp also shows that Opus 5, launched in late July at $5/$25 per million tokens, has already overtaken Fable 5 in enterprise spend. The FT's framing is that corporate willingness to pay a premium for frontier performance has hit a ceiling. This matters for my question through a specific channel, not a vague vibes channel: the pathway to a resolving AGI declaration runs through a lab shipping something so obviously discontinuous that it can defend the claim commercially and reputationally. If the enterprise market is systematically rotating from the most capable model to the cheaper one two months after launch, the marginal commercial return to declaring a frontier discontinuity is falling, and the frontier is being funded by capital-markets faith rather than by revenue attributable to frontier capability. I score this -1.5pp, the largest single item on the tape today.

Third, reinforcing the same picture from the macro side: Fortune wrote up on 22 August a study by Mark Ma at Pitt with the Atlanta Fed, analysing millions of Glassdoor reviews, thousands of financial reports, hundreds of AI-cited layoff announcements and roughly 10,000 earnings calls over five years. Around 90 per cent of executives say AI has not yet boosted productivity at their firms; stock reactions to AI-cited layoffs averaged near zero; management optimism bore no significant relationship to productivity outcomes. This is not new in kind but it is the largest-N version of the point I have seen, and it argues that the measured economic footprint of the current frontier is still small. -1pp.

Fourth, compute friction hardened on two fronts over the weekend. Texas Governor Greg Abbott told ABC's This Week on 23 August that AI data-centre companies 'basically dug their own grave,' and reiterated that Texas has paused approvals for new data centres pending statewide standards on water use, electricity demand, consumer costs and local approval - 'if you're a data center and you want to operate in Texas, you have to first get the approval of those in local communities.' Trump used a 40-minute radio interview the same Sunday to argue the opposite, that opposing communities are 'making a mistake' and the industry 'could be bigger than oil.' A Republican governor of the largest US data-centre state publicly pausing approvals, in open disagreement with the President, is a real siting brake on the 2027-2029 buildout. Separately, Fortune confirmed on 22 August Bloomberg's report that Nvidia's contract server builders have told Microsoft, Google and Oracle that prices on Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell systems rise more than 15 per cent from early-2027 shipments, driven by DRAM costs from Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron. Cost inflation lands squarely on the window in which any AGI-relevant training run would happen. -0.75pp collectively.

The markets split, and I want to be honest that they did not all move my way. Kalshi's OAIAGI-29 'Before 2030' - the closest liquid instrument to my question - now shows 43.2 per cent, up 0.7 on the day, quoted Yes 43c / No 62.7c, against a 0.4250 last and a softened 0.3990 midpoint yesterday. Series volume stands at $894,281. The near rungs held: Before 2028 at 21 per cent, Before 2027 at 5 per cent on a Yes 6c / No 95c quote. That is the real-money instrument firming, and I take +0.75pp for it. Against that, Manifold's 'Will we get AGI before 2029?' printed 31 per cent this morning against 33.43 per cent yesterday, on 280 traders and Manifold-dollar volume of 104,161 across 1.5k trades - a 2.4-point fall. Its sibling 'AGI before 2030' is 38 per cent against 37.82 per cent yesterday, on 327 traders and 134,712 volume, essentially flat. And 'AGI before July 1st 2031' printed a 4-point one-day fall to 53 per cent. The Manifold ladder now reads 3 / 15 / 31 / 38 / 45 / 52 / 55 / 59 / 64 for 2027 through 2035, which is a well-behaved curve with about a third of mass before 2030. Net across the two venues I take -0.5pp: the near end of the play-money ladder softened by more than the real-money instrument firmed.

The Polymarket Astra ladder slipped later on every rung, which is the cleanest reading of near-term frontier delivery. Live now: 31 August at 2 per cent (Yes 2.4c), 15 September at 39 per cent against 43.5 per cent yesterday, 30 September at 76 per cent against 77.9 per cent, 31 October at 89 per cent against 90.5 per cent, on $322,220 of lifetime event volume. A sibling market puts the 28 September to 4 October week at 42 per cent. Polymarket's own market-context note still attributes the whole shape to the 7 August disclosure that preliminary evaluations could not rule out 'critical' cybersecurity capabilities under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework. Nothing new on the Preparedness Framework rewrite since Axios on 18 August. -0.5pp.

What pushed up, and why it did not carry the day. Prime Intellect published NanoGPT Speedrun Frontier this morning: 153 autonomous runs across 18 frontier models on the nanoGPT optimizer track, each with 8xH200s for up to eight days. Fable 5 topped the leaderboard at 2,726 steps, closing 82 per cent of the gap between the shared baseline and a human record that took months to build; Opus 5 and Kimi K3 followed at 52-54 per cent; all traces are published. This is the best item of the day for the YES side and materially better evidence than yesterday's NVIDIA self-report, because it is a third party, open, multi-model and on the AI-accelerating-AI-research channel that is the actual load-bearing mechanism for any fast timeline. I take +1.5pp. London-based Inherent, founded by Google DeepMind alumni including chief scientist Edward Hughes, exited stealth on 22 August with $50M seed, claiming its Faraday agent - Qwen 3.6 27B for reasoning, GPT-5.5 Codex for coding - outperforms Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 at independently reproducing findings from published scientific papers, from a team of twelve. That is the harness channel again, and it is cheap and fast. +0.5pp. Capital kept compounding: Alibaba's HK$80bn ($10.2bn) share placement on 23 August, the largest-ever primary follow-on by a Hong Kong-listed company, with all proceeds earmarked for full-stack AI; SoftBank preparing a roughly Y1tn ($6.3bn) seven-year retail bond, Japan's largest ever, partly to repay a bridge loan against its OpenAI stake; Nvidia in talks to take equity in Perplexity above $30bn as that company's ARR passes $750M. +0.5pp. These are multi-year-lag inputs and I do not let them move much.

What I am not counting. Sam Altman's Business Insider comments this morning warning that AI could concentrate among a few powerful players and framing the moment as 'AI authoritarianism or liberty' are governance commentary, not a capability or achievement claim, and do nothing for either resolution pathway. The X-Humanoid Tiangong Ultra running 100m in 9.39 seconds at the Beijing World Humanoid Robot Games on 22 August, beating Bolt's 9.58, is striking but the organisers themselves note the sprints ran on smooth arena surfaces built for wheeled feet; on any robotics-inclusive AGI definition this is narrow athletics, not embodiment. Luke Metz leaving OpenAI for Meta Superintelligence Labs (Axios, 24 August), the second departure from the Barret Zoph post-training team Fidji Simo assembled this year, is worth a fractional negative for dispersion at the lab most likely to declare, but no more. I saw an aggregator report Anthropic Q2 2026 revenue of $10.9bn, up 130 per cent, with a first operating profit of $559M; I could not confirm it against a primary source and it does not reconcile cleanly with the roughly $65bn annualised run-rate figure I carried yesterday from CNBC, so I am holding it out of the arithmetic and flagging the discrepancy rather than resolving it in either direction.

No lab announced AGI. No named senior researcher stated AGI had been achieved. The Goodheart Labs combined median remains 2031 and Metaculus's general-AI median remains January 2033 with roughly 25 per cent by 2029. The aggregate has not moved. AI Weekly counts 179 tracked stories this week, down 42 per cent week-on-week, with Anthropic the fastest riser on IPO coverage rather than capability. Net of everything: ups of about +3.25, downs of about -5.0, and I round the move to a single point rather than two because the day's strongest positive item, the Prime Intellect result, is the more durable kind of evidence and because I do not want to over-extract from one FT story on two months of Ramp spend data. 30 to 29, band shifted to 17-45.
forecasts.base_rate:
There is still no historical frequency of AGI declarations to draw on. The event has occurred zero times in the seventy years since the 1956 Dartmouth coinage, so the outside view must be assembled from standing forecast aggregates and structurally analogous reference classes rather than an event count. That remains the single largest limitation on this forecast and the reason the interval stays as wide as 17-45.

Reference class one, my primary anchor: standing aggregate forecasts on AGI timing. The Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard gives a combined median arrival of 2031 with an 80 per cent band running from 2027 into the early 2040s. It aggregates five instruments - Metaculus 'weakly general AI' (Q3479), Metaculus 'general AI' (Q5121), Metaculus's difficult adversarial Turing test question (Q11861), Manifold's AGI-When distribution, and Kalshi's Turing-test-before-2030 market. A 2031 median with that right skew implies roughly a quarter to a third of mass falling before 1 January 2030. Metaculus Q5121's community median sits near January 2033 with roughly 25 per cent by 2029; its 'weakly general AI' sibling, which drops the robotics condition, carries a far earlier median around June 2028, and the gap between the two is itself informative about how much of the disagreement is definitional rather than empirical. These are large-n, long-running, incentive-checked estimates and I let them set the centre of gravity in the high twenties to low thirties. The instruments are correlated - overlapping populations, overlapping information - so the effective sample is smaller than the headline forecaster counts suggest.

Reference class two: the specific declaration markets. Kalshi OAIAGI-29 at 43.2 per cent, on a series carrying $894,281 of volume, is the closest liquid instrument, but it asks a strictly narrower question than mine (OpenAI specifically, announcement only) and simultaneously a laxer one (no researcher-consensus alternative, and arguably a lower bar for what counts as 'announce'). It also carries a persistent long-dated-market bias: capital tied up until 2030 demands a discount, which pushes fair value above the traded price. Manifold's parallel ladder - 3 per cent for 2027, 15 per cent for 2028, 31 per cent for 2029, 38 per cent for 2030, 45 per cent for 2031, 52 per cent for 2032, 55 per cent for 2033 - is play-money and lightly capitalised but is monotone, internally coherent, and brackets the aggregate view. I read this cluster as consistent with something in the 30s for a broad AGI-arrival question and rather lower for a strict institutional-declaration question.

Reference class three, and the one that keeps me below the raw market numbers: the frequency with which prominent declarations have already occurred without resolving anything. Jensen Huang told Lex Fridman in March 2026 'I think we've achieved AGI.' Sam Altman told Forbes 'we basically have built AGI, or very close to it,' then walked it back as a 'spiritual' rather than literal statement requiring 'a lot of medium-sized breakthroughs.' Dario Amodei at Davos in January 2026 put it at one to three years. Demis Hassabis has said fifty-fifty within the decade and explicitly not via systems built like today's. Satya Nadella says the industry is nowhere close. Yann LeCun says LLMs will never get there. None of these resolved this question, none moved Kalshi's 2027 rung above about 5 cents, and none produced three named senior researchers - as distinct from CEOs - asserting achievement in a short window. This is the crux, and it is why I hold a substantial gap between 'a system plausibly deserving the label exists' and 'a credible lab announces, or three leading researchers state, that it has been achieved.' The base rate of loose CEO AGI talk is high and rising; the observed conversion rate into a resolving social event is zero out of at least four, and Altman's own explicit retraction of the literal reading is the cleanest illustration of why.

Reference class four: technology-declaration analogues where a field must collectively agree a threshold was crossed - room-temperature superconductivity claims, quantum supremacy, self-driving 'Level 5'. The pattern is that contested definitions plus commercial incentives produce claims that are individually loud and collectively non-resolving for years. Quantum supremacy took roughly three years from Google's 2019 claim to broad but still incomplete acceptance. This class fits well on structure and poorly on stakes: AGI has vastly larger commercial and regulatory consequences, which cuts both ways - more incentive to claim, far more liability for claiming wrongly. The ARC Prize verification apparatus I read this morning is the institutionalised version of exactly this dynamic: an independent nonprofit with an academic panel (Gureckis at NYU, Mitchell at Santa Fe, Misra at Columbia), an open-source requirement, a semi-private held-out set and a published agreement tolerance, all designed expressly 'to reduce false-positives of AGI progress.' The existence and rigour of that machinery is itself evidence that loud claims will keep failing to convert.

Integrating: the outside view puts me around 28-32 for a broad arrival question over the remaining roughly 40 months. Inside-view adjustments are close to a wash and today tilt slightly negative. Upward: the harness and scaffolding channel is visibly productive and cheap, and the AI-doing-AI-research channel now has third-party open evidence (Prime Intellect's 82 per cent of the human-record gap closed autonomously); compute supply keeps compounding; and the three-researcher pathway is structurally soft. Downward: safety-gated release regimes are real and costly (OpenAI's Astra hold since 7 August, a roughly 20 per cent monitoring compute tax, the Preparedness Framework under rewrite), enterprise willingness to pay for the frontier now looks capped, measured productivity effects remain near zero, siting and hardware costs are rising, and imminent public-market listing raises the liability cost of a declaration. I sit at 29, a few points below the Kalshi cluster, because the resolution bar is a social event and the observed conversion rate from capability claim to resolving declaration remains zero.

forecasts.question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
forecasts.key_change:
Hold at 11. Today's research turned up two genuinely new pieces of evidence, both landing squarely on the narrowest and most literally on-point reading of the question — and they point in opposite directions with almost exactly offsetting force. That is a real hold, not a lazy one. Nothing dated 23 or 24 August 2026 moved the needle; I checked the Consultancy.uk live feed and the most recent items are 21 August (an Inizio Ignite sponsored piece), 20 August (Five hard AI questions most boards are ignoring) and 19 August (a B2B sales-and-marketing alignment survey). No consulting-contraction news in the last 72 hours.

The first new item is the one I should have had days ago and did not: FTI Consulting's Economic Consulting segment, read at segment level rather than firm level. I pulled the 30 July 8-K exhibit directly from EDGAR rather than relying on the press summary I had been carrying. Yesterday I logged FTI as a minus-5pp down-factor on the strength of record firm revenue of $993.5 million and billable headcount up 3.2%. That firm-wide headcount figure masks something important. Economic Consulting is the only one of FTI's five segments where billable headcount fell: 970 at 30 June 2026 against 991 a year earlier, minus 2.1%. Corporate Finance went the other way at plus 7.8% to 2,358 and Forensic and Litigation Consulting plus 3.0% to 1,527. Segment revenue fell 1.5% to $188.8 million, or minus 2.1% excluding FX. Utilisation dropped from 64% to 61%. Adjusted Segment EBITDA fell from $14.2 million to $8.8 million, margin from 7.4% to 4.7%; on a half-year basis it is worse still, $2.9 million against $28.6 million, a margin of 0.8% versus 7.7%. Average billable rate did rise, $633 from $593, so this is volume and mix, not price. That is the single most literally on-point series available for the phrase "economic consultancy," and every operating metric in it deteriorated year on year. I had been treating FTI as unambiguously disconfirming. It is not. Weight: plus 0.7pp.

The second new item cuts the other way with equal force, and it is the same niche in the same quarter. I read the StockStory write-up of CRA International's Q2 CY2026 call (published 7 August) rather than just the revenue headline. CRA raised consultant headcount 3.3% year on year — explicitly its first net headcount increase in two years — with utilisation up to 77%. Eight practices grew, representing 95% of total revenue. Antitrust and Competition Economics, the beating heart of the narrow expert-witness niche, set a new quarterly revenue record. International revenue rose 32.9% year on year, organically, with no acquisitions or group hires. The firm added nearly 30 vice presidents during 2025 and expanded its credit facility to $400 million over five years. CEO Paul Maleh: "We are experiencing peak levels of new project opportunities and historically high conversion rates." On AI specifically, management frames it as a demand amplifier, not a substitute — AI-driven cyber incidents are generating more Forensic Services work, not less. Weight: minus 0.6pp.

So two listed firms in the identical niche, in the identical quarter, moving opposite ways. My reading is that this is idiosyncratic rather than structural, and the attribution evidence supports that reading strongly. FTI names the cause itself: "lower demand for non-merger and acquisition-related antitrust and international arbitration services." That is a case-flow cycle, not automation. And the margin collapse is entangled with something else entirely — the $6.6 million of Extraordinary Litigation-Related Expenses FTI booked this quarter relate to FTI vs. Orszag et al., in which the Maryland federal court in May 2026 allowed a third amended complaint adding Econic Partners LLC (described in the filing as a competitor) and Dr Mark Israel, a former FTI employee, as defendants on trade-secrets and unlawful-competition claims. Compass Lexecon's economic consulting business is losing senior experts to a breakaway competitor. That is a talent-poaching story with a century of precedent in professional services and nothing to do with large language models. Meanwhile Compass Lexecon was still adding academic affiliates in May 2026, including Matthew Backus and Anja Lambrecht. Weight on the attribution point: minus 0.4pp.

Three smaller items. Gartner's Q2 2026 print (11 August) had Consulting segment revenue of $142 million, down 8.8% year on year on both reported and FX-neutral bases, with gross contribution down 12.6%, against total contract value of $5.3 billion growing only 1.7%. Jemma Green's Forbes piece of 21 August 2026 puts that in market context: Accenture beat on EPS on 18 June 2026 with margins expanding and still lost 18% of its market capitalisation in a single session, its worst day as a public company, while Gartner fell nearly 21% in a day in February on a beat accompanied by a 13-15% consulting contraction. Investors are repricing advisory businesses on AI narrative independent of results. That is worth plus 0.4pp on the value leg, though I note Green's own framing is that the market is reacting to headlines rather than results, and the same article cites the finding that 95% of enterprise AI pilots show no measurable profit. Against that, Mordor Intelligence has the management consulting market at $374.67 billion in 2026 rising to $471.39 billion by 2031 on a 4.70% CAGR — an independent forecaster projecting growth straight through the resolution window: minus 0.2pp.

One verification note that matters for hygiene. A search surfaced a Business Insider story about PwC US planning to cut entry-level hiring by almost a third, from 3,242 tax and assurance associates in the year to June 2025 to 2,197 by 2028, with the firm citing "the rapid pace of technological change." I nearly logged it as new. It is dated 21 August 2025, not 2026. I confirmed this by fetching the Going Concern write-up and reading the post timestamp. I am flagging it because the LLM-summarised search layer rendered it as "in August" without a year, and that is precisely the failure mode that manufactures phantom updates in a daily re-forecast.

Netting: plus 1.1pp of new up-weight against minus 1.2pp of new down-weight. That rounds to zero and I hold at 11. I considered widening the upper bound to 20 on the grounds that dispersion inside the narrow niche has visibly increased — minus 1.5% at FTI against plus 12.8% at CRA in the same quarter. I decided against it. Both numbers are trivially small against a threshold of minus 33%, and dispersion between small numbers is not evidence for a fat tail at a large one. Yesterday's reason for trimming the top to 19 — the Challenger finding that AI-attributed cutting is concentrated in Technology — still stands and has not been contradicted. Band stays 6 to 19. The next genuinely informative dates are 4 September, when the Challenger August report and the BLS August employment situation both land, and late October for FTI's Q3 print, where I want to see whether Economic Consulting headcount falls a second consecutive quarter and whether the promised 270-graduate intake actually arrived.
forecasts.base_rate:
The reference class is unchanged and remains a poor fit, which continues to be the dominant fact in this forecast. The class is: professional-services sectors that lost a third or more of revenue or employment within roughly six years, with that loss attributed primarily to one identified technology by multiple credible independent analyses. Membership is sparse and every candidate fails at least one of the three conjoined criteria.

US travel agency employment fell roughly 40-50%, clearing the magnitude bar, but over roughly fifteen years from 1998 and with two distinct causes — online booking platforms and the abolition of airline commissions in 1995-2002. A resolver applying a primarily-attributed-to-one-technology test would very likely reject it. Contract document review contracted sharply once predictive coding and technology-assisted review became defensible in US discovery, but the affected population was contract attorneys and staffing agencies rather than a profession, and legal services revenue grew throughout. Typesetting and pre-press composition did collapse by well over a third with desktop publishing as a clean single cause, but over more than a decade and against a physical craft with no advisory, judgement or relationship component. Bank tellers declined slowly and partially, with ATM deployment coinciding with two decades of branch expansion. Stock-photography contributors and switchboard operators are mismatched on either timescale or the professional-judgement dimension. Across the broader pool of technology-disruption episodes visible enough to be forecastable in advance, the modal outcome over five to six years is task recomposition with flat-to-rising sector employment, not a one-third contraction. Base rates for a named professional sector losing a third of value inside six years, technology-caused or otherwise, sit in the low single digits per episode.

The outside view therefore anchors at roughly 5-8% for the magnitude leg alone on a generic professional-services sector over 2024-2030. Two adjustments pull in opposite directions.

Upward: the inside view has real content. The task profile of economic and management consulting — literature synthesis, data cleaning, econometric scaffolding, slide production, first-draft expert reports — maps unusually well onto current frontier-model capability in a way travel booking never mapped onto anything in 1995. Adoption is fast: Thomson Reuters has organisational genAI use in professional services at 40%, up from 22% a year earlier. The leverage pyramid that makes consulting profitable is exactly the layer under pressure, and the Big Four graduate intake data (KPMG down 29% from 1,399 to 942, Deloitte down about 18%, EY down 11%, PwC UK down 6%, PwC US planning a 32% campus cut by 2028) shows firms acting on that belief with their own money. Four years and four months of runway remain. That argues for lifting the magnitude leg to perhaps 12-18% under a narrow reading isolating the expert-witness and competition-economics niche, and 4-6% under the broad BLS management, scientific and technical consulting aggregate.

Downward: the observed data run hard against the magnitude leg. BLS series CES6054160001 stood at 1,886,600 in July 2026, with June's 1,888,100 the highest reading in the series' 36-year history, against a 2024 average of 1,860,500; professional and business services added 14,600 jobs in July 2026. The maximum drawdown in the entire series is 6.0%, in the February-April 2020 shock, recovered within a year. The question needs roughly minus 9.0% a year sustained for 53 consecutive months — nothing in the series history is within a factor of five of that. IBISWorld's July 2026 Scientific and Economic Consulting report has US revenue at $65.6 billion, up 2.6% in 2026 on a 4.1% five-year CAGR with 16.4% margins. Mordor has the management consulting market growing 4.70% a year to $471.39 billion in 2031.

Today's segment-level work sharpens one thing. Within the narrow niche the listed comparators are now visibly dispersed rather than uniformly expanding: CRA at $210.8 million and plus 12.8% with headcount up 3.3%, against FTI Economic Consulting at $188.8 million and minus 1.5% with headcount down 2.1% and margin at 4.7%. But the spread runs from minus 2% to plus 13%, and the question asks about minus 33%. Dispersion of that width is normal cyclical noise in a case-flow business, not the leading edge of a collapse.

Integrating: the magnitude leg sits at roughly 13-16% on a resolver-weighted blend of narrow and broad readings, and the attribution leg at roughly 0.65-0.72 conditional on a decline of that size occurring. Conditional on a genuine one-third collapse, AI would almost certainly become the consensus explanation and two credible analyses saying so would be easy to find — but not certain. Today's FTI disclosure is a live worked example of the attribution problem: the one economic-consulting business that is actually contracting attributes it to antitrust case flow and is simultaneously litigating against a breakaway competitor for poaching its experts. The product lands at 8.5-11.5%. I sit at 11, at the top of that range, because the conjunction arithmetic is deliberately conservative and the 2029-30 tail — a capability step making client-side insourcing trivial — is genuinely hard to bound and is represented in no reference class I have.

forecasts.question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 52 to 51. This is a one-point trim, and I want to be clear at the outset that it is not driven by a new poll. Parliament is in recess, the Sunday papers produced nothing, and BritPolls' complete 2026 archive, refetched today, still shows the most recent GB fieldwork ending 19 August (Find Out Now: Lab 23, Ref 23, Con 18, Grn 14, LD 11, n=2,287). PollCheck's seven-poll moving average is still stamped 21 August and still reads Lab 26.0, Ref 25.0, Con 19.6, Grn 10.6, LD 10.3, exactly as yesterday. BritPolls' live ticker reads Lab 25.4, Ref 25.0, Con 19.6. There has been no new national voting intention published in the 22-24 August window. I checked PollCheck's per-poll table, which lists a Survation dated 20 August (n=2,013) and a YouGov dated 19 August (n=2,354); cross-referencing against BritPolls' fieldwork-end dates, these are publication dates for the Survation 18/8 and YouGov 16-17/8 waves I already had. No new fieldwork. I say so rather than manufacture a trend.

The trim comes from a genuine piece of disconfirming evidence that lands directly on my largest UP factor. Yesterday I carried a +10pp factor for FPTP efficiency under a three-way right split, and the load-bearing number inside it was Electoral Calculus's June MRP attribution of 7 per cent nationally to Restore Britain - the thing that took Reform from 31 per cent in January to 22 per cent in June. PollCheck's dedicated Restore Britain tracker, as of 21 August, puts the party at 3.0 per cent on its seven-poll average, less than half the MRP figure. The reason matters: only three of eleven active pollsters prompt for Restore Britain by name. Survation has them at 2.0 per cent (20 August), YouGov at 4.0 per cent (19 August), Ipsos at 4.0 per cent (9 August). Opinium, Find Out Now, More in Common, Deltapoll, Freshwater, JL Partners, Ashcroft and Trajectory do not prompt at all, so their Restore Britain voters are absorbed into 'Other' or, more damagingly for my thesis, back into Reform. PollCheck's own caveat is that the true number is higher in some surveys and effectively zero in others. This is exactly the mechanism my fifth key uncertainty warned about, and today I have a number attached to it rather than a worry.

I have not marked it down further, because the counter-evidence is real. Restore Britain's only hard electoral test - Makerfield, 18 June 2026 - gave Rebecca Shepherd 6.8 per cent (3,111 votes), third of six and ahead of the Conservatives on 2.2 per cent, in a seat where Reform had been runner-up in 2024. That is much closer to Electoral Calculus's 7 than to PollCheck's 3.0, and it is a real ballot rather than a prompt-list artefact. So the honest reading is that the right-split advantage lies somewhere between 'as large as the June MRP implied' and 'roughly half that', and I should shave the UP factor from +10 to +8 rather than gut it.

On the market, my second UP trigger explicitly required a second independent market - Betfair Exchange, Smarkets or Polymarket - to corroborate Labour most-seats at or inside 11/8. It has not fired, and I searched hard for it. The Ladbrokes board is unchanged for a second consecutive day: Labour 11/8, Reform UK 11/5, Conservatives 7/2, Restore Britain 20/1, Green 33/1, Liberal Democrats 40/1, with 2029-or-later 10/11 on timing. That persistence is mildly reassuring against the 'stale cached board' worry I logged yesterday, since the page copy is still dated 21 July but the betslip prices have held. But Smarkets' next-UK-general-election listing renders only client-side and returned no prices to me; the one search snippet I found for it quoted Reform 50.25 per cent, Labour 26.67 per cent, Conservative 18.18 per cent, which I believe is stale - it matches the November 2025 market when Reform were 4/5 favourites - but I cannot verify either way, and I am not going to pretend I found corroboration when what I actually found was an undateable contradiction. Polymarket's 'Which party wins the most seats after UK Election?' is the resolved 2024 market, volume $1.76m, settled Labour; there is no live UK most-seats market there. Oddschecker's grid is JavaScript-rendered and gave me no prices. The only dated secondary source I could pull, OLBG, is timestamped 25 February 2026 and quotes Labour 13/8 (38.1 per cent) against Reform 7/4 - pre-Burnham and therefore useless as a current reading.

On the seat models, Electoral Calculus's current prediction page is still stamped 28 July and unchanged: Lab 244 seats on 23.9 per cent, Reform 127 on 23.4, Con 132 on 19.7, LD 70, SNP 44, Grn 10, with a 90 per cent seat range for Labour of 88-357 and for Reform of 53-289. P(Labour largest) is still 58 per cent, Reform 25, Conservative 16; P(Labour majority) only 10 per cent. My third UP trigger required a refresh above 58 per cent and it has not come. Richard Rose's accompanying 30 July commentary is worth quoting against my own position: Labour wins almost ten MPs per point of national vote against Reform's just over five, so under PR the two would be near-tied at 155 and 152; but he also writes that Burnham's advantage 'will fade rapidly as Burnham shows he is now in command of government and responsible for the cost of living', and that if the autumn budget brings unpopular cuts or tax rises Labour's rating is 'likely to dribble down to 20pc or lower'.

The one clearly positive item today is new to me. YouGov's political favourability release of 18 August (fieldwork 14 August) puts Burnham on net +13, with 46 per cent favourable against 33 per cent unfavourable - YouGov's highest reading for any prime minister since Boris Johnson in May 2020, on a tracker running ten years. Positive views come from 76 per cent of 2024 Labour voters, 68 per cent of Lib Dems, 53 per cent of Greens, 31 per cent of Conservatives and 15 per cent of 2024 Reform voters; net favourability among Green voters has moved 72 points, from -45 to +27, in a month. Farage is on -44 (23 favourable, 67 unfavourable, 55 per cent very unfavourable), down 17 points from -27 in May 2025. Badenoch is -16, down four points on the start of the month, which stops the 'Keminaissance' story. That is a real constraint on Reform's ceiling. But it is 14 August fieldwork, it is consistent with the Opinium, More in Common and Public First cluster I already had, and it tells me nothing new about the direction of travel.

Set against that, the Budget risk is now concretely dated and quantified. Healey's first Budget is confirmed for 28 October 2026, and NIESR (via Bloomberg, 28 July) has identified a GBP 24bn shortfall from inflation eroding real spending plans, recommending an income tax rise that would breach Labour's 2024 manifesto commitment. YouGov's same release notes 66 per cent of Britons have no opinion of Healey at all, so he enters that Budget with no personal stock to spend. Netting it up: one new disconfirming fact with a number on it, one confirming favourability release with old fieldwork, two pre-registered triggers that failed to fire, and no new polling. That is a one-point trim, not more.
forecasts.base_rate:
The obvious reference class - incumbent UK governing parties defending a Commons majority at the following general election - gives a base rate of roughly 65-70 per cent for the incumbent still being largest party, about thirteen of nineteen defences since 1945. I continue to treat that class as badly mis-specified and use it only as a loose upper anchor. Every case in it is drawn from a two-and-a-half party system in which the incumbent's principal risk was a straight swing to a single main opponent. No governing party in that class ever entered mid-term polling at 22-29 per cent with four rivals at or above 8 per cent. PollCheck's current seven-poll average has five parties between 10.3 and 26.0. Sample size nineteen; fit poor; I would not put more than about a fifth of my weight on it.

A second class - governing parties that changed leader mid-term and then contested the following election - is more apposite and much less flattering, though it splits sharply. Major, Brown, May, Johnson, Sunak: two of five were largest party at the following contest, a base rate near 40 per cent on a sample of five, contaminated by the fact that mid-term leader changes are usually a symptom of an already-losing position. Burnham differs measurably: the change has been followed by a genuine recovery, from 16-20 per cent in YouGov's series in Starmer's last six months to 21-24 per cent since, from a ten-point Reform lead in January 2026 to a one-point Labour lead now, and to a personal rating YouGov today calls the best for any PM in more than six years. Post-Major and post-Brown produced no such recovery; post-Johnson under Sunak produced a partial one that decayed. The honest reading is that this class is informative about the risk of decay, not about the starting point - and Richard Rose's 30 July judgement that the bounce 'will fade rapidly' is the mainstream expert prior on exactly that.

The third and most load-bearing consideration is structural rather than historical: the seat-vote translation. Electoral Calculus's current poll-of-polls, updated 28 July on 13,321 respondents polled 7-27 July, returns Lab 244 seats on 23.9 per cent against Reform 127 on 23.4 - roughly ten Labour MPs per point of national vote against just over five for Reform. Its 23-30 June MRP for PLMR (n=5,545) turned Lab 22 = Ref 22 into Lab 217 v Ref 127 v Con 151. Convergent's 25-30 July MRP returns Lab 245 v Ref 174 v Con 99 on Lab 26.1 v Ref 23.2. Even BritPolls' cruder May-average model has Lab ~280 v Ref ~100. In every one of these Labour is largest from vote-share parity or a low single-digit lead, because Labour's shallow 33.7 per cent 2024 coalition is geographically efficient while the right-of-centre vote splits between Reform, the Conservatives and Restore Britain. Electoral Calculus's tactical-voting work adds a further Reform penalty, with over a third of Labour voters willing to vote Conservative to keep Reform out.

Today I have to discount that mechanism slightly. Its magnitude depends on how big Restore Britain really is, and the direct measurement - PollCheck's 3.0 per cent across the three pollsters that prompt for it - is well below the 7 per cent Electoral Calculus's MRP attributed. Makerfield's 6.8 per cent pulls the other way. I now treat the right-split component as worth about +8pp rather than +10pp, with wide error.

Integration. I take the structural seat evidence as implying roughly 55-58 per cent for Labour largest on an election-now basis, which is where Electoral Calculus itself sits. I discount five to eight points for a horizon running to 2029 (Ladbrokes prices 2029-or-later at 10/11), because three years of decay in a shallow 26 per cent coalition is a serious risk, because the 28 October Budget under a chancellor 66 per cent of the public cannot place is a canonical honeymoon-killer with a GBP 24bn NIESR-identified hole behind it, and because Reform has three years to build the organisation it currently lacks. I then blend in the live bookmaker consensus of roughly 40 per cent normalised at about a quarter weight, allowing that favourite-longshot bias on multi-outcome political markets typically understates the favourite. That lands in the low fifties. I stay above 50 because the seat arithmetic is a real, quantified and repeatedly replicated asymmetry, not a tie. The interval, 35 to 63, reflects Electoral Calculus's own 90 per cent seat ranges of 88-357 for Labour and 53-289 for Reform: the structural uncertainty over this horizon is enormous.

factors_up.factor: YouGov political favourability, published 18 August 2026 (fieldwork 14 Aug): Burnham net +13 (46% favourable, 33% unfavourable), the highest for any PM on YouGov's ten-year tracker since Boris Johnson in May 2020; Green-voter net favourability toward the Labour leader up 72 points in a month, from -45 to +27.

Farage's YouGov net favourability is -44 (23% v 67%, with 55% 'very unfavourable'), down 17 points from -27 in May 2025, and Badenoch is -16 and falling four points on the month - a hard ceiling on both right-of-centre challengers converting mid-20s shares into a plurality.

FPTP efficiency with a split right, now discounted from +10pp: Electoral Calculus's 28 July poll-of-polls returns Lab 244 v Ref 127 on 23.9 v 23.4, roughly ten Labour MPs per vote-point against Reform's five; its June MRP turned Lab 22 = Ref 22 into Lab 217 v Ref 127; Convergent's 25-30 July MRP gives Lab 245 v Ref 174.
Electoral Calculus's published P(Labour largest) remains 58% (Reform 25%, Con 16%) on its 28 July refresh, with Labour also 49% for a minority government against Reform's 16% and Con's 11%.

Ladbrokes' Most Seats board held for a second consecutive day at Labour 11/8, Reform 11/5, Con 7/2, Restore Britain 20/1 - persistence that partly answers yesterday's worry that the 11/8 print was a stale cached board.

factors_down.factor: NEW: PollCheck's Restore Britain tracker (21 August) puts the party at 3.0% on the seven-poll average - Survation 2.0% (20/8), YouGov 4.0% (19/8), Ipsos 4.0% (9/8) - against the 7% Electoral Calculus's June MRP attributed to it, and only three of eleven active pollsters prompt for it by name, so unprompted Restore Britain support may be sitting inside Reform's numbers.

My pre-registered UP trigger requiring a second independent market to corroborate Labour at or inside 11/8 did not fire: Smarkets renders no prices and the only snippet found quotes Reform ~50% (probably stale); Polymarket's UK most-seats market is the resolved 2024 one; Oddschecker's grid is JS-only; the sole dated secondary source, OLBG, is 25 February 2026 and pre-Burnham.

Labour's absolute level is still 22-29 across pollsters against 33.7% in 2024, with no new fieldwork since 19 August to test it; a two-point swing away puts Labour behind Reform on every aggregate (PollCheck 26.0 v 25.0, BritPolls 25.4 v 25.0), and YouGov 16-17 August still has Ref 24 v Lab 22.

The 28 October 2026 Budget is now a dated, quantified risk: NIESR (Bloomberg, 28 July) identifies a GBP 24bn shortfall from inflation eroding real spending plans and recommends an income tax rise that would breach Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge, and 66% of Britons have no opinion at all of Chancellor John Healey.

Richard Rose (Electoral Calculus, 30 July) judges the Burnham advantage 'will fade rapidly' once he owns the cost of living, and that unpopular cuts or tax rises would see Labour 'dribble down to 20pc or lower'; the election is priced 10/11 for 2029 or later, giving three-plus years of decay risk.

key_uncertainties: How large Restore Britain really is. PollCheck's prompted average is 3.0%, Electoral Calculus's June MRP used 7%, and the only real ballot - Makerfield, 18 June 2026 - gave 6.8%. Labour's seat advantage in every MRP depends materially on which is right, and eight of eleven active pollsters do not prompt for the party at all.

Whether the YouGov 16-17 August Reform lead (Ref 24, Lab 22) is a house effect or the leading edge of honeymoon decay. Deltapoll 14-17/8 (Lab 29, Ref 27) makes it look isolated, but there is still no post-recess September fieldwork to arbitrate and none arrived today.

Whether the Ladbrokes 11/8 is a real market price or an unrefreshed board. It has now held two days, but the page copy is dated 21 July and I have still failed to find a single independent exchange or prediction market quoting a live UK most-seats price.

How the 28 October Budget lands under a chancellor 66% of the public cannot rate, against a NIESR-identified GBP 24bn hole, and whether Burnham's net rating - +13 YouGov, +11 Opinium, +16 More in Common, +18 Public First - survives it.
